items.item: A future is fundamentally a value, not a running computation — the distinction the whole chapter depends on is that building one (even a complex one with captured state) performs no work at all; only a call to poll does.

at.step: Nothing. Polling is the only thing that ever runs it

items.item: The laziness of futures is not an implementation detail but the actual backpressure mechanism of async Rust: a system can construct and hold arbitrarily many futures without any of them consuming execution resources until something actually polls them.

at.step: That laziness is the backpressure

items.item: Poll::Pending is not merely informational — it is the half of a contract: returning it without arranging a later wakeup leaves the executor with no mechanism to ever poll that future again, demonstrated here as a genuine, reproducible hang under a timeout.

at.step: It hangs. Timed out on purpose to prove it

items.item: The correct pattern for a future waiting on external work (a timer, a socket, a signal from another thread) is to store the Waker it receives during poll and have whatever completes that external work call wake() on it — this is the entire mechanism by which 'external event happened' becomes 'poll me again'.

at.step: The fix: store the waker, call it when the work finishes

items.item: std::task::Wake is the standard, safe way an executor builds a real Waker without touching the unsafe RawWaker vtable: wrap the executor's own per-task wakeup state in an Arc, implement wake(self: Arc<Self>), and Waker::from converts it.

at.step: A waker is built from an Arc, using the standard library's own Wake trait

items.item: A minimal but complete executor needs only a runnable-task queue and a way to turn a woken task back into a poll call; no thread anywhere in that loop runs the future's logic on its behalf — the executor's own thread, calling poll directly, is the only thing that ever executes any of it.

at.step: Future, waker, scheduler, poll — run end to end, no hidden thread

items.item: poll should return quickly and should not block; if a call to poll is known to take a while, that work belongs on a thread pool instead, precisely because blocking inside poll would stall every other task sharing that executor thread.

at.step: Nothing. Polling is the only thing that ever runs it

items.item: Calling poll again after a future has already returned Ready is explicitly unspecified behavior by the trait's own contract (though never permitted to cause actual undefined behavior, since poll is a safe method) — a correct executor or combinator must never do this.

at.step: A value that does nothing until something asks

items.item: The future/waker/poll model is deliberately runtime-agnostic: nothing in this topic's executor, Delay future, or Wake implementation depends on any particular async runtime, which is why the same shape (not the same code) reappears, at a larger scale, inside Tokio's own scheduler.

at.step: Future, waker, scheduler, poll — run end to end, no hidden thread

items.item: A future representing a value computed elsewhere (a conduit, in the standard library's own phrasing) does not do the real work itself — its only job is to report readiness correctly and to hold the Waker needed to report a change in that readiness, which is exactly the separation this topic's Delay future and its conduit thread demonstrate.

at.step: The fix: store the waker, call it when the work finishes
